name: Oregon grape (Mahonia aquifolium)
short: Applied to the skin: itching, burning, rash and allergic-type reactions in a few trial patients; one review: minimal side effects; another: no serious adverse events. No by-mouth safety data found.
text: All the cited evidence concerns Mahonia aquifolium creams or ointments applied to the skin; no safety data on taking it by mouth were found. In a randomised, placebo-controlled trial in 82 people with psoriasis, who applied a bark-extract ointment to one side of the body and a placebo ointment to the other for an average of four weeks, adverse reactions such as itching, burning and allergic-type reactions occurred in four patients (the abstract does not say which ointment was involved). In a 12-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 200 people with psoriasis using a homeopathic cream containing a proprietary Mahonia aquifolium extract, side effects were infrequent (under 1%) and minor, most often rash, a burning sensation on application and staining of clothing. A systematic review and meta-analysis of topical single-plant extracts for psoriasis, five of whose 12 studies used Mahonia aquifolium, reported no serious adverse events, and a review of eight trials in psoriasis and atopic dermatitis described minimal side effects. A wider review of topical plant treatments for psoriasis, not limited to Mahonia, found the most common adverse effects to be local skin irritation, redness, itching, burning and pain. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
